children.text: Consider all pairs $$$s_i$$$ and $$$s_{n-i+1}$$$. There are 3 cases:
If $$$s_i = s_{n-i+1}$$$, nothing needs to be changed.
If $$$s_i = c$$$ or $$$s_{n-i+1} = c$$$, you can change the one that is not equal to $$$c$$$ to $$$c$$$ in one coin.
Otherwise, you will have to change both of them to $$$c$$$ for two coins.
Summing the costs for each pair gives the minimum answer. The solution runs in $$$O(n)$$$ time and uses $$$O(n)$$$ memory.
There are several methods to solve the problem. Consider the following solution:

Let $$$c_x$$$ be the number of occurrences of the number $$$x$$$ in array $$$a$$$. Iterate $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ and output all numbers $$$x$$$ such that $$$c_x$$$ is at least $$$i$$$, in decreasing order. Thus, the mode will always be the largest number. The complexity of the solution is — $$$O(n)$$$ or $$$O(n\cdot maxA)$$$, where $$$maxA$$$ is the maximum number in array $$$a$$$.
First, note that if the pirate decided to steal coins from pile $$$i$$$, then it is beneficial to steal all coins from that pile:
The coins in pile $$$i$$$ can be represented as $$$p\cdot g$$$.
The operation can be repeated $$$p$$$ times while there are still coins in the pile, and $$$g$$$ will not change.

Let the sequence of indices $$$i_1, i_2, \ldots i_k$$$ be the indices of the coin piles we robbed. Our task is to find such a sequence that $$$\gcd(x, a_{i_1}, \ldots a_{i_k}) \gt 1$$$, and the sum $$$a_{i_1} + a_{i_2} + \ldots + a_{i_k}$$$ is maximum.

The final value of $$$\gcd$$$ divides the number $$$x$$$ and all elements in the sequence. We will maintain an array $$$c$$$, where $$$c_p$$$ is the sum of all $$$a_i$$$ such that $$$a_i$$$ is divisible by $$$p$$$. The answer is the maximum $$$c_d$$$ over all divisors $$$d$$$ of the number $$$x$$$. The time complexity of the solution is $$$O(n\sqrt{maxA})$$$ or $$$O(n\log(maxA))$$$, where $$$maxA$$$ is the maximum value in the array $$$a$$$.
Let us consider how the operations work. Indices $$$i$$$ and $$$i + 2$$$ have the same parity. Therefore, we can arbitrarily rearrange elements at positions of the same parity among themselves.

Take any array $$$b$$$ of length $$$m$$$ that is a hill. Define $$$pos_x$$$ as the position of number $$$x$$$ in array $$$b$$$. The numbers $$$pos_n$$$, $$$pos_{n-1}$$$, $$$\ldots$$$, $$$pos_i$$$ for each $$$1\le i\le m$$$ must form a contiguous segment of numbers. Let us prove this by contradiction:
Suppose there exists an index $$$i$$$ for which the condition does not hold.

Then, there are at least two numbers among $$$i$$$ to $$$n$$$ such that there are smaller numbers between them. In this case, these numbers form at least one local minimum. But by the definition of a hill, there can be no local minima in it.

Let us check whether it is possible to make array $$$a$$$ a hill. Let $$$c_x$$$ be the position of number $$$x$$$ in array $$$a$$$. Since we can arbitrarily swap numbers at positions of the same parity, we can consider even elements of array $$$c$$$ as $$$0$$$, and odd elements as $$$1$$$. Now for every suffix $$$i$$$ of array $$$c$$$, the following must hold:
Let $$$cnt_0$$$ be the number of $$$0$$$s, and $$$cnt_1$$$ be the number of $$$1$$$s in suffix $$$i$$$.
The absolute difference between $$$cnt_0$$$ and $$$cnt_1$$$ must not exceed $$$1$$$, otherwise the elements from the suffix cannot be arranged as a contiguous segment.
If all conditions are satisfied, then the answer exists. The time complexity of the solution is $$$O(n)$$$.

Let us create an array $$$b$$$ of length $$$n - 1$$$. Let $$$b_i$$$ be equal to $$$1$$$ if $$$s_i\neq s_{i + 1}$$$, and $$$b_i$$$ be equal to $$$0$$$ otherwise. For a clean string $$$s$$$, the sum of the elements of $$$b$$$ is $$$0$$$. To make the string clean, we need to reduce all elements of $$$b$$$ to $$$0$$$. Consider the robot's operations on string $$$s$$$:
When inverting substring $$$s[l \ldots r]$$$, only $$$b_{l - 1}$$$ and $$$b_r$$$ change.
After inversion, the values of $$$b_{l - 1}$$$ and $$$b_r$$$ are also inverted.
In one operation, we can make $$$1$$$ or $$$2$$$ elements of array $$$b$$$ equal to $$$0$$$.

From this, it follows that the minimum number of operations required to clean the string is $$$\lceil \frac{sumB}{2} \rceil$$$, where $$$sumB$$$ is the sum of all elements in array $$$b$$$. Now, to know the power of the string, we need the sum of values $$$\lceil \frac{b_l + b_{l+1} + \ldots + b_{r - 1}}{2} \rceil$$$ over all $$$1\le l\lt r\le n$$$.

For substrings with odd sum of $$$b$$$, we can add $$$1$$$ to the sum to get rid of the ceiling. The number of substrings with odd sum of $$$b$$$ is the number of substrings with different first and last elements (that is, the first element is $$$0$$$ and the last is $$$1$$$, or vice versa). There are exactly $$$cnt_0\cdot cnt_1$$$ such segments, where $$$cnt_0$$$ is the number of $$$0$$$s and $$$cnt_1$$$ is the number of $$$1$$$s in the string.
It remains to compute the sum of $$$b$$$ over all segments. For this, consider the contribution of each $$$b_i$$$ to the total sum:
If $$$b_i$$$ is $$$0$$$, then it contributes nothing.
Otherwise, $$$i$$$ and $$$i + 1$$$ belong to exactly $$$i\cdot (n - i)$$$ segments.

Now we need to handle modifications. After an update, only $$$b_{i-1}$$$ and $$$b_{i}$$$ may change. These two elements can be updated manually. We also need to maintain $$$cnt_0$$$ and $$$cnt_1$$$ in the string. Thus, we obtain a solution in $$$O(n + q)$$$ time and $$$O(n)$$$ memory.

It can be observed that the value of $$$\max(a) - \min(a)$$$ decreases quickly. This happens because the highest bit in the array disappears after $$$1$$$ or $$$2$$$ operations. Let us prove this as follows:

Let $$$c_0$$$ be the number of elements of the array that do not contain the highest bit, and $$$c_1$$$ be the number of elements that contain the highest bit. Denote $$$p$$$ as the sum of $$$\frac{c_0\cdot (c_0 - 1)}{2}$$$ and $$$\frac{c_1\cdot (c_1 - 1)}{2}$$$. There will be exactly $$$p$$$ pairs of indices $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ such that $$$a_i\oplus a_j$$$ does not contain the highest bit. The value of $$$p$$$ is minimized when $$$c_0=\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor$$$ and $$$c_1=\lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil$$$.

For $$$n$$$ at least $$$6$$$, the value of $$$p$$$ is not less than $$$n$$$. Therefore, when $$$n$$$ is at least $$$6$$$, the highest bit disappears after the transformation. When $$$n=5$$$, the highest bit disappears in at most $$$2$$$ operations:
If $$$c_0$$$ is $$$2$$$ or $$$3$$$, then after the next transformation $$$c_0$$$ becomes $$$4$$$.

One can implement transformations in $$$O(n^2\log (n))$$$ and apply them until all elements of the array become $$$0$$$. The complexity of the solution is $$$O(n^2\log (n) \log (A))$$$, where $$$A$$$ is the maximum element of the array $$$a$$$.
Moreover, it can be observed that the number of transformations until the array becomes zero does not exceed $$$9$$$.
First, read the explanation for F1.
You need to be able to perform transformations faster than a naive enumeration of all pairs. There are several ways to do this; let us consider a solution using a trie (prefix tree).

Implement a function $$$get(i, k)$$$ that, for each $$$i$$$, can find the $$$k$$$-th smallest $$$a_i\oplus a_j$$$ among all $$$j$$$ (not necessarily greater than $$$i$$$). Create an array $$$cnt$$$ of length $$$n$$$, where initially $$$cnt_i = 0$$$ for each $$$1\le i\le n$$$. Now for the transformations:
Choose the minimum among them and add it to a vector. After adding it, increase $$$cnt_i$$$ by $$$1$$$.
Since $$$a_i\oplus a_j$$$ is added twice, perform exactly $$$2n$$$ additions. After that, replace the array $$$a$$$ with the elements of the vector at odd positions.
Thus, the transformations take $$$O(n\log(A))$$$ time. The total complexity is $$$O(n \log^2(A))$$$ time and $$$O(n\log(A))$$$ memory.

Let $$$I$$$ be the set of all positive numbers $$$x$$$ such that $$$m \& x = x$$$. First, let us try to find the number of paths to position $$$n$$$. We will define a dynamic programming array where $$$dp[i]$$$ is the number of paths of length $$$i$$$. Obviously, $$$dp[i]$$$ is equal to the sum of $$$dp[i-x]$$$ over all $$$x \in I$$$.

A straightforward brute force solution would take up to $$$O(n^2)$$$ time, so we introduce an auxiliary array $$$st$$$ for optimization. Let $$$st[i][j]$$$ be the sum of $$$dp[i-x]$$$ over all $$$x$$$ such that $$$x \lt 2^j$$$ and $$$x \in I$$$. Consider the transitions:

Now let us return to counting the costs. We will add the contribution of each $$$c_x$$$ to the answer for all $$$x \in I$$$. Notice that every path that includes a move of length $$$x$$$ has the form $$$0 \rightarrow ... \rightarrow i \rightarrow i+x \rightarrow ... \rightarrow n$$$ for some $$$0 \le i \le n-x$$$. The number of such paths is $$$dp[i] \cdot dp[n-i-x]$$$. But this is still $$$O(n^2)$$$ time.

If we remove the move of length $$$x$$$ from a path that includes it, we obtain a path of length $$$n - x$$$. Suppose such a path has exactly $$$p$$$ jumps. Then this path can be extended in $$$p+1$$$ ways by placing the move of length $$$x$$$ before or after each of the moves. For a fixed $$$x$$$, we need to know the sum of $$$p+1$$$ over all paths of length $$$n-x$$$, after which we can multiply this value by $$$c_x$$$ and add it to the answer. For this, we compute another dynamic programming array $$$cnt$$$, where $$$cnt[i]$$$ is the sum of $$$p+1$$$ over all paths of length $$$i$$$. The transitions in $$$cnt$$$ are identical to those in $$$dp$$$, except that we need to add $$$dp[i]$$$ to $$$cnt[i]$$$ at the end, since the number of moves in each path increases by one.
It remains only to add $$$c_x \cdot cnt[n - x]$$$ to the answer for all $$$x \in I$$$. Thus, the solution works in $$$O(n \log n)$$$ time and memory.
